title: Pollinator and thief interaction with flowers of Malpighiaceae species in temporal networks: seasonality reshapes network structure and species roles
content:
Abstract
Neotropical Malpighiaceae flowers produce oil as a main and essential resource for most bees of the Centridini, Tapinotaspidini, and Tetrapediini tribes. Interactions between these flowers and floral visitors form networks structured along a specialization–generalization continuum. However, network structure may vary with flowering seasonality and visitor behaviour, including pollinators and thieves. Here, we provide the first quantitative assessment of seasonal changes in Malpighiaceae-floral visitor networks, incorporating different functional roles. All networks were significantly modular and specialized, but not nested, indicating a structured yet non-hierarchical organization. Network structure shifted across seasons and functional roles, suggesting that the balance between mutualistic and antagonistic interactions is dynamically reorganized over time. Contrary to expectations, networks were not primarily structured by oil-specialist bees. Instead, generalist Meliponini bees played central roles in maintaining connectivity, whereas oil-bees were less influential, with only a single Epicharis species contributing to modularity. The predominance of peripheral species and few highly connected nodes indicate limited functional redundancy, potentially increasing vulnerability to species loss. Overall, our findings show that Malpighiaceae networks are driven by the interplay between generalist and specialist species, emphasizing the importance of including antagonistic interactions to understand ecological network organization and stability.
